Meyers said Millar Western will also look at filling vacancies at other company operations with displaced employees. “For those who will continue to work, the period between now and your final day of employment will be considered as working notice,” he said. According to the letter, to qualify for severance, employees must remain active until their last scheduled day of work.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, ends Banff rescue-dog program
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments and discontinue its Banff search-and-rescue dog program as part of $145 million in cuts over three years. The agency sent workforce-adjustment notices to 2,917 employees and says it will make individual decisions in the coming weeks. The Canadian Avalanche Rescue Dog Association and British Columbia Search Dog Association have urged the agency to reverse the cancellation, warning it could weaken rescue capacity. Parks Canada says it will shift wardens to a regional model focused on high-risk areas and that wardens can enforce park law without dogs. The associations say they are working on a short-term volunteer response during avalanche season.

items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

items.title: [pbs.org] Super El Niño nears December peak as extreme weather spreads
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The exceptionally strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is intensifying weather risks across several regions, including heavy rain and flash floods in the U.S. Southwest. Scientists say the pattern adds moisture to the air and shifts winds, making downpours more likely, although it is not the sole cause of individual storms. The World Meteorological Organization expects the event to peak in December and persist into February 2027. The agency says it could rank among the strongest since at least 1950. Flooding has also been reported in Peru and Ecuador, while Indonesia and parts of Southeast Asia are unusually dry. In the Southwest, flooding prompted evacuations, and the San Juan River threatened Pagosa Springs, Colorado. Warmer oceans linked to human-caused climate change may amplify the event’s effects, but scientists caution that separating El Niño’s contribution from the long-term warming trend remains difficult. In September, sea-surface temperature in the Pacific’s Niño 3.4 reference region reached 29.70°C, while the global ocean average for that month, excluding polar waters, set a September record of 21.05°C. Forecasters expect the strongest effects to continue into 2027.

items.title: [npr.org] Alaska Native villages remain displaced a year after Typhoon Halong
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong destroyed homes and infrastructure in western Alaska, residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok remain displaced as repairs continue, with many unsure when they can return. The October 2025 storm affected more than 40 communities, and about 1,500 people were evacuated from Kwigillingok, Kipnuk and Nightmute. Alaska officials estimate that federal aid will make most Kipnuk homes livable by Thanksgiving, but say some residents need replacement housing. The state is seeking more funding. Both Kipnuk and Kwigillingok voted to relocate to higher ground, but current disaster funding is not designed to pay for moving the communities.

items.title: [latimes.com] El Niño-linked floods force Southwest evacuations; Arizona declares emergency
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Pacific storm systems brought torrential rain and flooding across the normally arid Southwest, prompting evacuations in Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. The National Weather Service said El Niño was disrupting weather patterns as the region faced another round of heavy rain. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs declared a statewide emergency Monday to help local authorities clear roads, repair infrastructure and assist displaced residents. At least one person died in the flooding; police said a second death in Flagstaff appeared weather-related, pending an official determination. Former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue estimated that more than 20 trillion gallons of water fell across the Four Corners states and Nevada over two weeks. Flooding damaged roads and bridges, stranded residents and caused sewage to back up into some homes. Although rain had ended in parts of the Southwest by Monday, flooding along some swollen waterways could continue through at least Tuesday.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. items.title: [space.com] NASA Swift telescope faces uncontrolled reentry after failed orbit rescue
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to reenter Earth’s atmosphere in the coming days after a failed attempt to raise its orbit. Forecasts place reentry roughly between Nov. 3 and Nov. 6, but the timing and location remain uncertain. The U.S. Space Force is tracking the 1.5-ton spacecraft. Most of it is expected to burn up, although some dense tungsten components and mirror parts could survive. The possible reentry corridor spans a broad band near the equator, much of it over ocean. Solar activity increased atmospheric drag and accelerated the telescope’s orbital decline. Swift, launched in 2004 for a two-year mission, detected more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars and rapidly alerted other observatories to transient events. It continued observations after the rescue attempt was abandoned, but NASA shut down its systems in late October when its low orbit made stable operations impossible.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Colonel Joshua Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, installing the seventh of eight planned solar arrays. Kutryk became the fifth Canadian astronaut to walk in space. Astronaut Jenni Gibbons served as capsule communicator, and Canadarm2, the station’s robotic arm, supported the installation. Kutryk and Menon are scheduled to install the final array during another spacewalk on Nov. 5.

items.title: [livescience.com] NASA's Swift telescope burns up after nearly 22 years
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

items.title: [cisa.gov] U.S. agencies warn hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Five U.S. agencies warned on Nov. 5 that hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, including controllers used by grocery stores, hospitals, food producers and transport operators. Attackers may exploit unpatched or internet-accessible devices to change temperatures or defrost settings, or prevent operators from seeing temperature readings. Such attacks could spoil stock, compromise storage safety and damage equipment. The warning follows attacks on European supermarkets on Nov. 2 and an incident that altered refrigeration settings at three French blood-service facilities. The U.S. agencies did not say whether refrigeration systems in the United States had been targeted. They urged operators to remove unnecessary internet access, secure remote connections, update firmware, isolate control systems from business networks and set alerts for unsafe temperature changes.

Hundreds of residents left Russian-occupied Oleshky on Friday as Russian and Ukrainian officials completed a joint evacuation and aid operation under a local truce, the first such mission since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. The ceasefire, brokered with help from U.S. first lady Melania Trump and supported by Pope Leo XIV, allowed food and medical supplies into the frontline town; officials have not confirmed the total number evacuated. People headed for Ukrainian-controlled areas were taken first to Anapa in southern Russia and were then due to fly to Belarus and travel by bus into Ukraine. The circuitous route avoids mined roads along the front line. More than 1,000 residents, many elderly, remained in the town, according to a report from the scene; they received food, medicine, hygiene supplies and fuel. The truce is due to end late Sunday, Nov. 1. The Russian and Ukrainian human rights commissioners have asked Melania Trump to help coordinate recurring relief missions, while peace talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States are expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in early November.

items.title: [36kr.com] EU sues IBM, Atos and Leonardo over border system delays
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The European Union has sued IBM, French IT group Atos and Italian defence contractor Leonardo over repeated delays in developing its Entry/Exit System (EES), an electronic border-check system for the 29-country Schengen area. The EU agency eu-LISA filed the civil case in Estonia in December 2025; the dispute became public on Monday. The agency and the European Commission say the case concerns development delays, not the system’s current operation. The system was initially scheduled to launch in 2022 but was not fully rolled out until 2026. Its introduction caused hours-long airport queues after fingerprint scanners malfunctioned, including when exposed to sweat. Some countries are still acquiring scanners. The system records fingerprints and photographs from non-EU travellers on their first entry to help identify visa overstayers and identity fraud. eu-LISA says the case does not affect operations. Estonia’s Harju County Court has accepted the case, but no hearing has been held or scheduled.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology (phys.org, elpais.com, scientificamerican.com, lavanguardia.com). One U.S. official said the action followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft; Iranian state media reported five explosions on the island and said residents saw two aircraft overhead. The Wall Street Journal reported that the strike was part of a series of smaller, previously undisclosed U.S. attacks in recent weeks. Officials said the operations were intended to counter threats to U.S. forces and commercial shipping without signaling that Washington was resuming major combat. The Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been heavily disrupted since the war began in February, is a key oil route. Oil prices fell more than 7% on Monday as expectations of a deal grew. President Donald Trump said a settlement with Tehran “could happen,” and Vice President JD Vance said talks had made progress. Iran’s foreign minister said indirect discussions were underway through mediators. U.S. officials said further talks were planned this week to pursue a framework linking an end to Iranian attacks in the strait with the lifting of the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports.
